overview: The H-60 Tempest Bomber is a heavy bomber whose design philosophy reflects the industrial and strategic priorities of First Order (34 ABY–). First Order Tempest bombers carried magma bombs in wing racks for planetary suppression campaigns. Production estimates place the class at ~400 units, though wartime losses, capture, and black-market duplication make precise fleet registries unreliable.
history:
Engineering teams first finalized the H-60 Tempest Bomber blueprints during the political climate of First Order (34 ABY–). The heavy bomber was intended to solve specific fleet gaps—whether planetary assault, convoy escort, starfighter superiority, or terror bombardment—and shipwrights iterated hull plates, reactor output, and crew compartments accordingly.

Once deployed, the H-60 Tempest Bomber appeared in fleet actions that defined its reputation. First Order Tempest bombers carried magma bombs in wing racks for planetary suppression campaigns. Combat logs show crews exploiting the class's strengths while improvising fixes for known weaknesses under fire, a pattern repeated across every major galactic conflict.

As doctrine evolved, rival factions studied captured H-60 Tempest Bomber hulls. Refit yards duplicated weapons mounts and sensor suites; some variants never appeared in official manifests. Estimated production of ~400 units therefore understates how many similar silhouettes operated under alternate insignia.

Surviving H-60 Tempest Bomber vessels now sit in museum orbits, mercenary fleets, and scrap worlds. Historians treat the class as a measure of how galactic wars industrialize violence—each hull a factory product that outlived the politicians who ordered it.
significance:
The H-60 Tempest Bomber demonstrates how heavy bomber design shapes campaign outcomes. Its layout influenced successor programs and remains a case study in naval academies.

With roughly ~400 units hulls associated with First Order (34 ABY–), the class became a visual symbol of its faction's reach—recognizable in holonet footage and feared in convoy manifests.

Engineers still debate whether the H-60 Tempest Bomber prioritized firepower over crew survival; that trade-off defines its legacy in both propaganda and honest after-action reports.
